mem.t: These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life, and that you may continue to believe in the name of the Son of God.

lessons.title: Assurance Built on a Promise
lessons.theme: The assurance of salvation rests on God’s word, not on our feelings

v: The testimony is this: that God gave to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.
He who has the Son has the life. He who doesn’t have God’s Son doesn’t have the life.
These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life, and that you may continue to believe in the name of the Son of God.
“Most certainly I tell you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and doesn’t come into judgment, but has passed out of death into life.

lessons.still: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up, like someone receiving a gift that has already arrived. Slowly say three times: “He who has the Son has the life.” Each time you say it, hand the Lord one “what if I’m not good enough?” thought.
teach: When you fly, a lurch in your stomach doesn’t convince you that you are no longer on the plane. Whether you are on board depends on your boarding pass and the aircraft, not on how you feel. The spiritual life works the same way: feelings are like the weather, sunny one day and rainy the next, but assurance must be built on a foundation that does not change.

John states his purpose plainly: “that you may know that you have eternal life.” Not “hope,” not “guess,” but “know.” On what basis? “He who has the Son has the life.” Eternal life is not a thing; it is found in a Person. Jesus himself said that whoever believes “has passed out of death into life”—he speaks of it as already done.

The order of assurance is: fact → faith → feeling. God’s word is the locomotive, faith is the coal car, and feeling is only the last carriage. Put feeling at the front and the whole train goes nowhere. Change your mindset and you change your life: move from “Do I feel saved?” to “What has God said?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Scripture is my standard. Assurance does not rest on my feelings or performance but on God’s word. Making feelings the standard puts “me” at the center; making God’s word the standard lets God be God. The self-ruled person is often dragged about by emotions; the self-emptied person rests in God’s faithfulness.
q: Who is God? — What kind of God writes his promises down because he wants you to “know”?
Who am I? — Does your assurance of salvation usually rest on feelings, on performance, or on God’s word?
How shall I respond? — Today, when doubt rises up, which verse will you answer it with?
lessons.jesus: Jesus never left people living in guesswork. To the repentant thief on the cross he said, “Today you will be with me in Paradise.” That man had no time to do good works or make amends—only a faith that turned toward Jesus—yet he received the clearest promise of all. Assurance comes from Jesus’ words, not from our résumé.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that you do not leave me living in guesswork and anxiety. You said that whoever has your Son has life—so I have life. When my feelings waver, bring me back to stand firm on your word. I do not rely on my own performance, but only on the finished work of Jesus. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write 1 John 5:13 on a card and put it where you will see it often
Write down one feeling that often makes you doubt your salvation, and next to it write a promise from Scripture
Tell a brother or sister in Christ: “I know I have eternal life, because…”
lessons.noon: “He who has the Son has the life.” — Lord, right now I look not at my feelings but at your word.

lessons.title: No One Can Snatch Them
lessons.theme: The Good Shepherd holds his sheep and never lets go

v: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.
I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.
My Father who has given them to me is greater than all. No one is able to snatch them out of my Father’s hand.

lessons.still: Make a loose fist with one hand, then wrap your other hand around it. Picture the Father’s hand enfolding Jesus’ hand, with you held in the middle. Be still for a minute and say to the Lord, “I am in your hands. I am safe.”
teach: When a small child crosses the street, his safety does not depend on how tightly he holds his father’s hand but on how tightly his father holds his. Small hands get tired and let go; the big hand does not. Much of believers’ anxiety comes from constantly checking whether their own grip is tight enough, while forgetting to look at the great hand that is holding them.

Jesus describes his sheep with three marks: they “hear my voice,” “I know them,” and they “follow me.” Then come three guarantees: “I give eternal life to them,” “they will never perish,” and “no one will snatch them out of my hand.” More wonderful still, the sheep are in the Son’s hand and also in the Father’s hand—two hands, double protection. “No one” includes Satan, circumstances, and even your own weakness.

The sheep’s safety lies not in the sheep’s strength but in the shepherd’s faithfulness. This is no license for careless living, because true sheep hear the shepherd’s voice and follow him. Assurance and following are two sides of one coin: the more we listen to his voice, the more we know we belong to him; the more we know we belong to him, the more gladly we follow.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The focus is on Jesus, not on myself. The self-ruled person builds security on how tightly he holds on; the self-emptied person entrusts his security to the Good Shepherd. Letting Jesus reign includes letting him take responsibility for keeping me. My place is to listen and follow; his place is to hold and protect.
q: Who is God? — The Father’s hand over the Son’s hand: how does this picture help you understand God’s keeping power?
Who am I? — Do you often find yourself checking whether you are “holding on tightly enough”?
How shall I respond? — In what matter today will you quietly listen for the Good Shepherd’s voice?
lessons.jesus: Before his suffering, Jesus prayed to the Father that he had kept all those the Father had given him (John 17:12). When the soldiers came to the garden to arrest him, he stepped forward and told them to let his disciples go (John 18:8). The Good Shepherd always stands between his sheep and danger—and in the end he laid down his life for them.
lessons.pray: Jesus, Good Shepherd, thank you that you know me and hold me in your hand. My hands grow weak, but yours never let go. Make my ears more familiar with your voice and my steps more willing to follow you. Today I rest in your hands. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Pray a “hands-enfolded” prayer, asking the Lord to keep everything in your day
Before making a decision today, pause and ask, “Lord, what do you say?”
Send John 10:28 to a friend who is feeling discouraged
lessons.noon: “And no one will snatch them out of my hand.” — Lord, right now I am secure in your hands.

lessons.title: The Spirit Bears Witness
lessons.theme: God’s Spirit within me cries, “Abba, Father”

v: For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!”
The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God;
and if children, then heirs— heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him, that we may also be glorified with him.

lessons.still: Quietly and slowly say one word: “Abba.” Add nothing else, just as a child in the dark night calls out, “Daddy.” Notice the settled peace that rises in your heart—that is the Holy Spirit bearing witness within you.
teach: Some adopted children, even after taking a new surname and moving into a new home, still hide bread under their pillow at night, afraid there will be nothing to eat tomorrow. Legally they are sons and daughters, but inwardly they still live like orphans. Many Christians are the same: their identity has changed, but their mindset is still afraid.

Paul contrasts two spirits: “the spirit of bondage again to fear” and “the Spirit of adoption.” The slave’s heart asks, Have I done enough? Will I be thrown out? But the child’s heart can cry, “Abba! Father!”—a name of intimacy and trust. What is more, “the Spirit himself testifies with our spirit”: God’s word bears witness from the outside, and the Holy Spirit bears witness from within. When outside and inside agree, we know for certain that we are God’s children.

The Spirit’s witness is not a quest for some mystical emotional high; it is a growing sense of being a child of the family. When we fail, we want to come home instead of running away; when we pray, we dare to speak honestly; when we see our brothers and sisters, we feel we are one family. And this witness brings the hope of heirs—suffering with him today, glorified with him tomorrow.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Holy Spirit is my guide. He lives in the heart, not in the head. Living from the head keeps calculating “Am I good enough?”—the more we calculate, the more troubled we become. Living from the heart by the Spirit, we can call “Abba, Father” in peace—the more we lean on him, the more joyful we become. Moving from a slave’s heart to a child’s heart is exactly the change of mindset we need.
q: Who is God? — God is willing to be called “Abba” by you. What does that reveal about his heart?
Who am I? — At what moments do you still live like a slave afraid of being thrown out?
How shall I respond? — How will you draw near to your heavenly Father as his child today?
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane, at his moment of deepest anguish, Jesus prayed, “Abba, Father” (Mark 14:36). In the darkest night he still used the most intimate name. Today he gives us that same name and that same Spirit, so that we become heirs together with him.
lessons.pray: Abba, Father, thank you for giving me the heart of a child. I will no longer serve you out of a slave’s fear. Holy Spirit, bear witness ever more clearly in my heart, so that even when I am weak I dare to come home, and even in the night I can still call out to you. Being your child is my greatest blessing. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Three times today, softly call out in your heart, “Abba, Father!”
Write down one “slave mindset” thought and rewrite it as a “child mindset” sentence
Say something to a family member that makes them feel, “You belong here with us”
lessons.noon: “The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God.” — Lord, right now I come near to you with the heart of a child.

lessons.title: Still a Child When I Fall
lessons.theme: Sin breaks our fellowship but does not change our relationship

v: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin. If anyone sins, we have a Counselor with the Father, Jesus Christ, the righteous.

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on one failure from today or yesterday. Don’t cover it up, and don’t keep beating yourself up over it. Hand it over like a bundle of dirty laundry and say, “Lord, I was wrong.” Then take a deep breath and receive his cleansing.
teach: If a child breaks a vase, is he still his parents’ child? Of course. But that evening he may not dare to meet their eyes, and the mood around the dinner table changes. The relationship has not been broken, but the fellowship has been damaged. Only when he says, “I’m sorry—I broke it,” does laughter return to the home.

John writes to “my little children”—a family word. He hopes they will not sin, and he also provides a way back: “If anyone sins, we have a Counselor with the Father.” The word “confess” carries the sense of “saying the same thing”—standing on God’s side and seeing the matter as he sees it. God forgives on the basis of his being “faithful and righteous.” Jesus has already paid the price, so forgiveness is not God being casual about sin; it is God being just.

Before we sin, Satan says, “It’s no big deal.” After we sin, he says, “You’re finished.” Both are lies. The truth is that sin is serious—so serious that Jesus had to die; and grace is greater—so great that when we confess, we are cleansed. Don’t treat failure as a reason to leave; treat it as the road home.
lessons.light: 321 Light: When the proud fall, they cover up, make excuses and blame others—that is the self-ruled life protecting itself. The humble confess and return to their place, letting God be God. Humility is the key to revival: confession is not losing face but arriving back at the door of the Father’s house.
q: Who is God? — God’s forgiveness is “faithful and righteous.” How does that shape the way you see your own failures?
Who am I? — When you fall, is your first reaction to hide, to justify yourself, or to come home?
How shall I respond? — Is there something you need to say “I was wrong” about today, to God or to someone else?
lessons.jesus: Peter denied the Lord three times, then went out and wept bitterly. Yet the risen Jesus prepared a charcoal fire and breakfast for him on the shore and asked him three times, “Do you love me?” (John 21). Jesus did not revoke Peter’s calling; instead he entrusted him again: “Feed my sheep.” A disciple who has failed is still a disciple.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, I confess that I often fall, and I often want to hide from your gaze. Thank you that Jesus is my advocate and that your forgiveness is faithful and righteous. I bring my failures to you now; please cleanse me. I will no longer listen to the lie that says “You’re finished.” I am coming back to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Before bed, take three minutes to review your day, and confess specifically to God any sins that come to mind
Say “I’m sorry” to someone you hurt with your words today
Memorize 1 John 1:9 and meditate on it once more before you sleep
lessons.noon: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins.” — Lord, right now I come back to you.

lessons.title: Assurance Brings Freedom
lessons.theme: We do not serve in order to be saved; we serve because we have been saved

v: For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers,
nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.

lessons.still: Think of a recent pressure in your ministry or work, and lay it before the Lord. Quietly tell yourself, “I am not doing this in order to be loved, but because I am already loved.” Let your shoulders slowly relax.
teach: Picture two students, both studying hard. One already knows he has been accepted; the other is still waiting for the results. Their frame of mind is completely different: the first studies in order to learn, the second studies in order to prove himself. Service without assurance is often like the second student—the more we do, the more tired and afraid we become.

At the end of Romans 8, Paul lists in one breath ten things that might separate us, and his conclusion is: none of them can. For this love is “in Christ Jesus our Lord,” firmly anchored in Christ. So he says, “be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work.” Assurance does not make us lazy; it makes us wholehearted, because “your labor is not in vain in the Lord.”

This week we have walked a path: assurance built on God’s word → held in the Good Shepherd’s hand → the Spirit’s witness → still a child when we fall → and today, serving freely from a place of assurance. Next week we will learn to “meditate day and night” on God’s word, so that this assurance can sink its roots ever deeper.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-ruled service is about proving ourselves and winning approval; self-emptied service is for Jesus and for others. Because our salvation is settled, we don’t need to grab glory; we can let Jesus receive all the glory. Service that flows from assurance is the foundation for building what belongs to God.
q: Who is God? — “Nothing will be able to separate us from God’s love.” How secure is this God’s love?
Who am I? — How much of your service is about proving yourself?
How shall I respond? — This week, what act of service will you do in the freedom of being “already loved”?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was baptized, before he had performed a single miracle, a voice from heaven said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). He went out to serve from the Father’s affirmation, not in order to earn it. In him, we too set out from that same love.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that your love holds me fast and that nothing can separate me from you. Free me from the burden of “serving in order to be loved.” Let me set out from assurance and abound in your work freely and joyfully. All glory be to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Read Romans 8:38–39 aloud, adding the thing you fear most to the list
Do one act of service and seek no one’s praise afterward
Share with a spiritual companion one way you have become more certain of your salvation this week
lessons.noon: “Nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.” — Lord, right now I serve freely in your love.
